speaker: A
text:
Let’s start with a story.

The first time the moon disappeared, everyone blamed the clouds. The second time, people checked their telescopes. The third time, a woman named Ada checked her coat pocket.

There it was, warm as a boiled egg.

She took it to the lost-property office at the train station.

“Any identifying marks?” the clerk asked.

Ada turned it over. On the far side, in a child’s handwriting, someone had written: *Please don’t put it back until I’m asleep.*

speaker: B
text:
The clerk read the note twice.

“How long have you had it?”

“Since half past nine.”

“And it’s still warm?”

Ada nodded.

“Then they’re still awake,” he said, and took off his glasses.

From beneath the counter he brought out a biscuit tin lined with a folded tea towel. Ada set the moon inside. The clerk reached for the lid, hesitated, and left it propped open a little.

“Some children,” he said, “can’t sleep in the dark, either.”

They waited. The last train came in carrying a man with flowers and nobody else. The man stood on the platform for a while, then sat down with the flowers across his knees.

At eleven, the moon began to cool.

“There we are,” the clerk whispered.

But as Ada lifted it out of the tin, she saw a second line of writing, so faint she had to turn the moon toward the desk lamp.

*If he comes back, tell him I tried to stay awake.*

Ada looked out at the platform. The man had unwrapped the flowers and was picking off the bruised petals, one by one.

“Leave the lid open,” she told the clerk. “I’ll be right back.”

speaker: A
text:
“Have I missed her?” the man asked.

Ada sat beside him. “She tried to stay awake.”

He nodded as if this were something he’d been told before and had never quite learned how to answer.

“I said I’d be there before bedtime.”

“Were you on the last train?”

“I was on the one before it, too. I got off at the wrong station.” He looked down at the flowers. “I used to know the way.”

In the office, the clerk turned off the desk lamp. A narrow stripe of light from the biscuit tin fell across the platform.

The man gathered the flowers.

“Will you tell her I came?”

Ada looked at the clock. It was seven minutes past eleven. Beyond the station the houses were dark, but she could see, in the thin light from the tin, the footpath that ran behind them.

“You can tell her in the morning,” she said. “Come on. Which house?”

He started to say the number, stopped, and then smiled a little.

“There’s a yellow chair by the back door. Unless she’s moved it.”

They found the chair on its side in the wet grass. He put it upright and sat down, still holding the flowers.

Above the roof, the moon rose. Through an open window Ada heard a child turn over, then settle again. The man heard it too. He took his hand away from the doorbell.

speaker: B
text:
“Will you remember the way next time?” Ada asked.

He looked back. From the garden she couldn’t see the station, only the gap in the hedge where they’d come through.

“Maybe not,” he said.

Ada went back to the office for a lost-property tag. On one side she drew the path from the station, with a cross where the hedge opened. On the other she drew the chair. She tied it to the string around the flowers.

He studied the drawing. “It’s yellow,” he said.

“I haven’t got a yellow pencil.”

“No, that’s all right. I remember the yellow.”

In the morning the girl came out in her socks. She took the flowers from his lap and put them on the step.

“You can ring,” she told him. “I’m awake now.”

So he got up and rang, and she went inside to let him in.

speaker: A
text:
That evening, the clerk found the lost-property tag on the counter. Someone had colored the chair yellow, going a little over the lines.

On the back, beside the cross, the girl had written: *We’re cutting the hedge on Saturday. I’ll leave the gap.*

speaker: B
text:
On Sunday, on his way to open the station, the clerk went to see.

The hedge had been cut square and flat. Where the path met it, there was a gap wide enough for a man carrying flowers.

From the path he could see the yellow chair. There was another chair beside it now, with a saucer on the seat to keep the rain out of a cup.

speaker: A
text:
As he turned to go, the girl came out and took the saucer off the cup.

“He’s not coming till Tuesday,” she said.

The clerk stopped. He hadn’t asked.

“He told me himself,” she said, and carried the cup inside.

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday the clerk saw him get off the quarter-past four. He had no flowers this time. He stopped by the office and took a scrap of paper from his pocket.

“Would you tell me if I’ve got this right?”

On it he’d drawn the station, the path, and the gap in the hedge. Beyond the gap were two chairs.

“That’s right,” said the clerk.

The man folded the paper and put it back in his pocket. A little later, through the open office window, the clerk heard a doorbell ring.

speaker: A
text:
The clerk reached up to close the window. Before it shut, he heard the bell ring again.

Then, faintly, the girl said, “I know. I’m coming.”

speaker: B
text: The clerk left the window open while he counted the till. A little later he heard the two chairs scrape on the paving stones. Then he heard nothing for a while, and counted the sixpences again.

speaker: A
text:
When he locked up, the moon was already over the hedge.

He put the biscuit tin back under the counter. He’d meant to take the tea towel home to wash, but it was clean enough for another night.

speaker: B
text: He went out by the platform door. At the bend in the path he could see the two cups on the step. Someone had put a saucer over each.

speaker: A
text:
From inside the house he heard the man say, “Shall I leave the hall light on?”

“Yes, please,” said the girl.

By the time the clerk reached the bend, the light was coming through the little window above the door.

speaker: B
text: The next morning, when the clerk came by, the hall light was still on. As he passed the gap in the hedge, someone inside switched it off.

speaker: A
text:
A moment later the back door opened.

“Tuesday again?” the girl asked.

“Thursday,” the man said. “I wrote it down.”

“All right,” she said. “I’ll put your cup out Thursday.”

speaker: B
text:
At the station, the man took out his scrap of paper to check the time of his train. Thursday was written across the bottom, beneath the two chairs.

As he waited, he drew a cup on the seat of one of them. Then he drew another.

speaker: A
text: When the train came, he folded the paper along its old crease. Then he opened it and folded it the other way, so that Thursday was on the outside.

speaker: B
text:
On Thursday it rained. The girl brought the cups in and set them on the kitchen table.

When the bell rang, she called, “Come round the back. It’s open.”

A moment later, from the hall, he said, “I’m already round the back.”

She’d been listening for the front bell all afternoon. She went into the hall and showed him where to hang his coat.

speaker: A
text:
There was a peg low enough for her to reach. His coat hung almost to the floor.

“We can have our tea in here,” she said. “I moved the chairs.”

He looked into the kitchen. The yellow chair was beside the stove.

“Where shall I sit?”

“In the other one,” she said. “The yellow one’s mine.”

speaker: B
text:
He sat down. From the other chair he could see the gap in the hedge.

“Milk?” she asked.

“Please.”

She brought the jug over with both hands. He moved his cup nearer the edge of the table so she could reach it.

speaker: A
text:
A little milk went into the saucer.

“That’s all right,” he said.

“I know,” she said. “I’m getting a cloth.”

When she came back, he had taken the scrap of paper out of his pocket. She wiped the table around it.

“You can draw the peg,” she said, “if you think you’ll forget.”

He looked through the kitchen door at his coat.

“I think I’ll remember where my coat goes.”

She hung the cloth over the back of her chair. “You can leave it there till after tea, anyway.”

speaker: B
text:
After tea, she took the cups to the sink. He folded the paper and went to get his coat.

“Wait,” she said. “It’s still raining.”

He stood in the hall with one hand in his sleeve. Then he took the coat off again and hung it on the low peg.

“Shall I dry?” he asked.

She handed him the cloth from the back of her chair. “That one’s for spills,” she said, and got him a dry one.

speaker: A
text:
He dried the cups and put them in the cupboard.

“Not so far back,” she said. “I can’t reach.”

He moved them to the front of the shelf, their handles turned out. By then the rain had stopped, but she handed him a spoon.

speaker: B
text:
He dried the spoon and opened a drawer.

“Not that one,” she said.

He shut it and tried the one below. There were the spoons.

“Will you put the kettle on?” she asked.

He looked at the two cups at the front of the shelf.

“Again?”

“I didn’t have any,” she said. “I was pouring yours.”

speaker: A
text:
“What do you have?”

“Milk. But I like it warm.”

He took down both cups. While the kettle heated, she fetched the milk jug and set it beside him.

“How much?” he asked.

She put her finger halfway up the side of her cup, then moved it a little higher.

“I can reach it from here,” she said, and pulled her chair closer.

speaker: B
text:
He warmed the milk in a little pan. When he lifted it to pour, she put her finger back on the cup.

“There,” she said.

He stopped a little short.

“You can have the bit in the pan,” she said.

He poured it into his own cup and sat down. From where she’d moved the yellow chair, she could see out through the gap in the hedge, too. The station lights had come on.

“Is that your train?”

“One of them,” he said, and took a sip.

speaker: A
text:
The train pulled away while they were drinking.

“When’s the next one?” she asked.

He took out the paper and looked. “Six twenty.”

She looked at the kitchen clock. It had stopped at ten to four.

“Can you reach that?” she asked.

He stood on the floor and lifted it down. She watched while he put in a battery from the drawer with the spoons.

“What time shall I make it?”

He looked at his watch. “Five past six.”

“Put it a little lower when you put it back,” she said. “Then I can do it next time.”

speaker: B
text:
He held the clock against the wall while she reached up to touch the bottom of it.

“There,” she said.

There wasn’t a hook that low, so he set it on the windowsill. The second hand went all the way round while they finished their milk.

At quarter past, she brought him his coat.

“Is that enough time?”

“If I go now.”

She opened the back door. He put on his coat and went as far as the gap.

“Tuesday?” he called.

She looked at the clock through the kitchen window, though it couldn’t tell her that.

“Tuesday,” she said.

speaker: A
text:
She washed the cups and put them at the front of the shelf.

A little later she heard the train go by. The kitchen clock said six twenty-one.

She left it as it was.

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday, when the bell rang, the kitchen clock said four twenty-one. She took the cups down before she went to let him in.

He hung his coat on the low peg. From the kitchen she heard him pat one pocket, then the other.

“I’ve left my paper at home.”

“Did you need it?”

He looked back at the door, as if he could see the way he’d come.

“Not today,” he said.

speaker: A
text:
She put the kettle on. He went to the drawer with the spoons and took out two.

“Only one,” she said. “I’m having milk.”

He put one back. Then he took the little pan down from its hook.

“How much was it?”

She held up her cup and showed him.

speaker: B
text:
He poured a little less than she’d shown him and set the pan back on the stove.

“There’s more if you want it.”

She took a sip. “That’s enough.”

Outside, the quarter-past train pulled away. He turned to look.

“That’s the one you came on,” she said.

“Oh,” he said, and put his teaspoon in his saucer. “So it is.”

speaker: A
text:
“Did you get a seat?” she asked.

“By the window. I saw your yellow chair.”

She looked at the chair she was sitting in. “From the train?”

“Just for a second.”

She set her cup down and shifted the chair a little nearer the window.

“See if you can see it going back,” she said.

speaker: B
text:
On the way back he sat on the other side of the carriage. As the train went past the gap, he saw the yellow chair and, just above the back of it, her hand.

He lifted his own, though he wasn’t sure she could see through the glass.

On Thursday she said, “I saw your sleeve.”

speaker: A
text:
“I waved,” he said.

“I thought you did.”

When it was time to go, he put on his coat and went out through the gap. She climbed onto the yellow chair to wait for the train.

It was still light enough to see him all the way to the platform. Before he got on, he turned and waved.

She had both hands on the back of the chair. She let go with one.

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday, she was standing at the window when the train came in. He got off and waved before he went through the station gate.

She waved back. Then she climbed down and put the kettle on. By the time he rang, she had both cups on the table.

speaker: A
text:
He hung up his coat and came into the kitchen.

“What are you looking for?” she asked.

“The pan.”

She pointed to the stove. She’d already poured the milk into it.

He turned on the burner. “Tell me when.”

She came and stood beside him. When the first little bubbles gathered at the edge, she said, “Now.”

speaker: B
text:
He turned off the burner. She moved her cup closer, and he poured.

“Have I left you any?” she asked.

He tipped the pan to see. “A little.”

She fetched his cup. There was just enough milk to cover the bottom. He poured his tea on top, and she carried the pan to the sink.

speaker: A
text:
“Leave it to soak,” he said.

She ran a little water into it and came back to the table.

“Did you see me wave?”

“I saw you climb down.”

“That was after.”

“Then I’ll look sooner on Thursday,” he said.

speaker: B
text:
On Thursday he looked before the train had passed the hedge. The yellow chair was empty. Then he saw her by the station gate, waving with both hands.

When he came through the gate, she put one hand in his.

“I haven’t put the kettle on,” she said.

“We can put it on when we get there.”

speaker: A
text:
At the bend he started to let go of her hand.

“What is it?” she asked.

“I can see the gap from here.”

“I know,” she said, and kept hold of his hand.

speaker: B
text:
At the gap she went through first. There was room for them both, but not quite side by side. He thought she’d let go then. She put her hand behind her instead, and he followed her through.

At the back door she stopped.

“Have you got the key?” he asked.

“It’s open,” she said. “I’m waiting for you to ring.”

speaker: A
text:
He rang. She opened the door and went in ahead of him.

“Come in,” she called from the hall.

Only then did she let go of his hand, so he could take off his coat.

speaker: B
text:
He hung his coat on the low peg. From the kitchen came the sound of the cupboard opening.

“Tea?” she called.

“In a minute,” he said. “Come and look.”

Through the little window above the door she could see the moon. She reached for the light switch and turned the hall light off.

They stood there until the kettle began to rattle.

speaker: A
text:
She switched the light back on.

“Did you put the kettle on?” he asked.

“Before I went to meet you,” she said. “I forgot to turn it on.”

“Then who did?”

“I did. Just now, when I got the cups.”

He nodded. “I thought I’d missed something.”

“Only that,” she said, and went to make the tea.

speaker: B
text:
When he came into the kitchen, she was standing by the stove.

“The milk’s nearly ready,” she said.

He took the pan off when she told him. She held her cup steady while he poured.

“You can pour the rest in mine,” he said, and passed her the pan.

She did, holding the handle with both hands. A little went into the saucer. He got up for the cloth, and she moved his cup so he could wipe underneath.

speaker: A
text:
She took a sip from her cup.

“Too hot?” he asked.

“A little.”

He started to get up for the milk jug, but she put her cup down.

“We can wait,” she said.

So he sat back, and they watched the steam go.

speaker: B
text:
When she tried it again, he looked up.

“Is it right now?”

She nodded. He picked up his own cup and found that he’d been waiting too.

speaker: A
text:
When they’d finished, she took both cups to the sink. He picked up the dry cloth.

“Is it Tuesday next?” he asked.

“Yes.”

He reached for his coat pocket, then remembered his coat was in the hall.

“Write it here,” she said.

She took the calendar down from beside the stove and laid it flat on the table. He found Tuesday and wrote his name. She took the pencil and wrote hers underneath.

speaker: B
text:
She hung the calendar back beside the stove. The pencil was still in her hand.

“Shall I leave it here?” she asked.

He opened the drawer with the spoons. There was room beside them.

“There,” she said. “We’ll both know where it is.”

speaker: A
text:
On Tuesday the bell rang while she was putting the spoons away.

She left the drawer open and went to let him in.

“Thursday next?” he asked over tea.

“Thursday,” she said, and he went straight to the drawer for the pencil.

speaker: B
text:
He took down the calendar and wrote his name in the square for Thursday. Then he left it flat on the table and set the pencil beside it.

She finished her milk before she wrote hers.

“Do you want me to tell you when it’s time for the train?” she asked.

“Yes, please.”

She looked at the clock on the sill. There were nine minutes before he needed his coat.

She put the pencil away and sat down again.

speaker: A
text:
After a while he said, “Is it time?”

“Not yet.”

He picked up his cup, though it was empty. She took it from him and set it beside hers.

When it was time, she told him. He went to get his coat, and she left the cups where they were and went with him as far as the gate.

speaker: B
text:
At the gate he asked, “What did we say?”

“Thursday.”

He put his hand in his coat pocket.

“It’s on the calendar,” she said.

He took his hand out and waved. She waved back, though he hadn’t gone through the gate yet.

speaker: A
text:
“Thursday,” he said again, and went through.

At home she washed both cups. Before she put them away, she took the calendar down to see whether there was room in Thursday’s square for anything else.

There was, but she couldn’t think of anything they needed to remember.

speaker: B
text:
On Thursday the bell rang while she was at the sink. She dried her hands and went to the door.

“I didn’t see you at the window,” he said.

“I was washing the pan.”

He hung up his coat. In the kitchen the pan was upside down on the draining board. He turned it over and went to get the milk.

speaker: A
text:
There was only a little milk left in the jug. He poured it all into the pan.

“What about yours?” she asked.

“I can have it without.”

She took the jug and opened the fridge. There was a full bottle in the door.

“I meant you could open this one,” she said. “The lid’s tight.”

He opened it and poured some into the jug. She put the bottle back.

“Now we’ve got some for Tuesday,” she said.

speaker: B
text:
He set the jug on the table and turned on the burner.

“Tuesday at the same time?”

She nodded and took down the calendar. When he opened the spoon drawer, the pencil rolled to the back. He reached in for it.

“Leave it at the front when you’re done,” she said.

He wrote his name and set the pencil beside her cup.

“I meant in the drawer.”

“I know,” he said. “You haven’t done yours yet.”

speaker: A
text:
She wrote her name and put the pencil beside the spoons, close to the front.

“You don’t have to write yours,” he said. “You’re here anyway.”

“Not at the station,” she said.

He looked at the calendar again. “At the gate?”

“Unless it’s raining.”

He reached for the pencil, then shut the drawer.

“If it’s raining, I’ll ring.”

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday it was raining when the train came in. She watched it from the yellow chair, then got down and put the kettle on.

By the time he rang, the rain had stopped.

“I could have met you,” she said.

“You can walk me back.”

She took his coat and hung it on the low peg. “If it’s still stopped,” she said.

speaker: A
text:
When it was time, she opened the back door and held out her hand, palm up.

“Nothing,” she said.

He brought her coat from the hall. She put it on, and they went through the gap.

Halfway to the station it began to rain again. He stopped and looked back.

“Keep going,” she said. “We’re nearer your end now.”

speaker: B
text:
They stood under the platform roof. Rain dripped from his sleeve onto her hand.

“You’ll get wet going back,” he said.

“I’m wet now.”

When the train came, he got into the carriage and found a window seat. She stayed under the roof until he waved. Then she put both hands in her pockets and went home.

speaker: A
text:
At home she hung her coat on the low peg. It dripped onto the floor, so she fetched the cloth from the kitchen.

On Thursday, when he came to hang up his coat, hers was still there.

“Where shall I put mine?” he called.

“On top of mine,” she said. “Is it wet?”

“Not today.”

“Then I’ll come with you again.”

speaker: B
text:
When it was time, he took both coats off the peg and brought hers into the kitchen.

At the station gate she held out her hand to see if it was raining. He put his hand in it.

“Only checking,” she said.

But she kept hold until the train came.

speaker: A
text:
On the train he found the old scrap of paper in his coat pocket. He unfolded it on his knee.

There was room to draw a gate between the station and the path. He had no pencil.

He folded the paper again. The pencil was in the drawer with the spoons.

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday he took the pencil from the drawer and drew the gate.

“Is that so you’ll remember where it is?” she asked.

“No,” he said. “It’s where you wait.”

She leaned over the paper. “On this side,” she said, and put her finger down.

He gave her the pencil. She made a dot where her finger had been.

speaker: A
text:
“Will you take it with you?” she asked.

He folded it and put it in his pocket. Then he put the pencil back beside the spoons.

On Thursday she waited on the other side of the gate. The man stopped when he saw her.

“I thought you waited over there.”

“I do when I’m seeing you off,” she said, and took his hand.

speaker: B
text:
At the bend he asked, “Shall we put another dot?”

She thought about it. “You can, if you like.”

After tea he took out the paper. He looked at the dot she’d made, then drew a short line through the gate to the other side.

She turned the paper around.

“That’s the way back,” she said.

speaker: A
text:
He turned it back again.

“And that’s the way here.”

She looked at it from her side of the table. “You can leave it like that.”

When it was time for the train, he folded the paper and put it in his pocket. At the gate she went through with him.

“Just this once,” she said. “I want to see which window you sit at.”

speaker: B
text:
He chose a seat and put his hand against the glass. She stood opposite him until the train started to move.

The next window went past, and then the next. At the last one she waved again.

On Tuesday he asked, “Did you see where I sat?”

“Yes,” she said. “But you can sit somewhere else if you want. I know what to look for now.”

speaker: A
text:
On the way back he found a seat on the far side of the carriage. When the train started to move, he leaned across the empty seat beside him to wave.

On Thursday she said, “I nearly missed you.”

“I can sit by the window next time.”

“No,” she said. “Just wave a little longer.”

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday he waved until the platform ended. By then she was too far away to see his hand, but she could still see his sleeve moving.

On Thursday he asked, “Was that long enough?”

“Yes,” she said. “I’d stopped before you did.”

speaker: A
text:
“What did you do then?”

“I went home.”

He nodded and drank his tea.

“I left the hall light on,” she said. “I could see it from the bend.”

speaker: B
text:
That evening he waited at the gate while she walked back. At the bend she turned and waved. He waved back, then went through to the platform.

When the train passed the hedge, the hall light was still on. He could see it from his seat without leaning across.

speaker: A
text:
On Tuesday, when he came through the gate, she was looking back toward the house.

“I left it on,” she said.

“I can see.”

She took his hand. “I thought I’d try it this way round.”

speaker: B
text:
At the bend she asked, “Could you see it from the train?”

“Not from where I was sitting,” he said. “I saw you, though.”

At the back door he rang. She let him in and switched off the hall light while he hung up his coat.

speaker: A
text:
When it was time to go, he put on his coat and reached for the switch.

“Are you coming to the gate?” he asked.

She nodded.

“Shall I leave it on?”

She put on her coat. “Yes,” she said. “I’ll turn it off when I get back.”

speaker: B
text:
At the gate he waited for her to start back.

“You can go through,” she said. “I know the way.”

He went through. She waited until he turned around, then waved and set off.

When the train passed the hedge, the hall light was off. In the kitchen window she was standing on the yellow chair, waving.

speaker: A
text:
On Thursday he asked, “Did you have to hurry?”

“A little,” she said. “The chair was already there.”

When it was time for him to go, she stayed in the kitchen.

“Not coming to the gate?”

“Not today.”

He went out, then came back as far as the open door.

“Will you wave?”

She put both hands on the back of the yellow chair. “I’m getting up now.”

speaker: B
text:
He went through the gap without looking back.

When the train came past, she was still on the chair. She saw his hand first, then his face.

She waved until the last window went by. Then she climbed down and pushed the chair back to the table.

speaker: A
text:
On Tuesday she was sitting in the yellow chair when he rang.

“Did you see me come in?” he asked.

“No,” she said. “I heard the bell.”

He hung up his coat and came into the kitchen. She’d left the other chair pulled out for him.

speaker: B
text:
He sat down.

“Did you want me to look?” she asked.

“I wondered if you’d seen.”

“I was reading,” she said, and showed him how far she’d got.

He went to put the kettle on. She finished the page before she got up for the cups.

speaker: A
text:
He brought the pan to the table and poured her milk. She put a finger between the pages to hold her place.

“What’s happening?” he asked.

She looked down at the book. “I’d have to start a bit further back.”

“All right,” he said, and moved his cup out of the way so she could lay the book flat.

speaker: B
text:
She turned back two pages, then one more.

“Here,” she said. “This is where he gets on the wrong bus.”

She began to read. Halfway down the page she stopped to drink her milk.

He kept his finger on the line.

speaker: A
text:
She set her cup down and began again where his finger was.

At the bottom of the page she stopped. “He still doesn’t know he’s on the wrong bus.”

“Does somebody tell him?”

“I haven’t got that far,” she said.

He lifted his finger so she could turn the page.

speaker: B
text:
A little later the clock on the sill clicked. She looked up.

“You’ve got five minutes.”

“Is that enough for another page?”

She looked at the page. There was a picture at the bottom.

“Yes,” she said, and began.

speaker: A
text:
At the bottom of the page the boy got off the bus.

“Is that where he meant to go?” he asked.

She looked at the picture. “I think he just wanted to ask somebody.”

He went to get his coat. While he was in the hall, she slipped a scrap of paper into the book.

“What’s that for?”

“So I don’t read on by mistake,” she said.

speaker: B
text:
“Thursday?” he asked.

She nodded. A corner of the paper stuck out of the book. He took the pencil from the spoon drawer and wrote Thursday on it without pulling it out.

On Thursday, after he hung up his coat, she opened the book.

“You can read this bit,” she said. “I’ll get the cups.”

speaker: A
text:
He began to read. At the cupboard she stopped with one cup in her hand.

“Wait till I sit down,” she said. “I want to hear what he asks.”

He kept his finger on the line while she brought the cups over. Then he went back to the beginning of the sentence.

speaker: B
text:
“‘Does the bus go back the way it came?’” he read.

“Does it?” she asked.

He looked down at the next line.

“Wait,” she said, and went to turn off the kettle. When she came back, she pulled the yellow chair around to his side of the table.

“Now I can see, too.”

speaker: A
text:
He read the next line. “‘This one doesn’t,’ said the driver. ‘But there’s one coming the other way.’”

In the picture there was a bus stop across the road. She put her finger on it.

“Does he see it?”

He looked at the line below, then moved his hand so she could see it too.

“You read that bit,” he said.

speaker: B
text:
“‘I can wait with you,’ said the driver.”

She looked at the picture again. “He hasn’t got off,” she said.

“Not yet.”

She turned the page. There was another picture. The bus was still there, but the driver was standing beside the boy.

“He did,” she said, and moved the book a little nearer so he could see.

speaker: A
text:
He looked at the picture. “He left the door open.”

“So he can get back in,” she said.

They read to the place where the other bus came. Then she put the scrap of paper between the pages.

“Shall I write Tuesday?” he asked.

She looked at the clock on the sill.

“We’ve got time to see if he gets on.”

speaker: B
text:
She took the paper out again. On the next page the boy was on the bus. The driver was still at the stop.

“He waited,” she said.

The man looked at the picture. “He’s waving.”

“No, that’s his ticket,” she said, and brought the book closer.

In the next picture the boy had put the ticket in his pocket. His hand was up against the window.

“There,” she said. “Now he is.”

speaker: A
text:
He turned the page. The next one was blank.

“Does he get home?” he asked.

She looked at the back of the book, in case there was another picture.

“It doesn’t say.”

The clock clicked on the sill. He went to fetch his coat.

“Shall I take the paper out?” she called.

“Leave it there,” he said. “I’d like to see that last picture again.”

speaker: B
text:
On Tuesday she opened the book to the last picture before he took off his coat.

“Look,” he said. “The driver’s waving too.”

She bent over the page. At the very edge, beside the bus stop, there was a hand she’d taken for part of the sign.

“You can only see his fingers,” she said.

He went to hang up his coat. She left the book open while she got the cups.

speaker: A
text:
When he came back, she’d moved the book to the windowsill beside the clock.

“Are we reading it again?” he asked.

“Not today,” she said. “I just wanted to leave it open.”

He brought the milk to the table. As she reached for her cup, a draught turned the page.

He set the pencil across the corner to hold it down.

speaker: B
text:
When it was time to go, she took his cup to the sink.

“Shall I shut the window?” he asked.

“Leave it a little bit open.”

He pulled it in until the page stopped lifting. Then he put the pencil back in the drawer.

speaker: A
text:
At the back door he put on his coat.

“Will you wave?” she asked.

He looked back at the yellow chair. It was still on his side of the table.

“Yes,” he said.

She stayed at the sink. A little later she heard the train go by through the open window. She lifted one wet hand.

speaker: B
text:
On Thursday he asked, “Were you at the window?”

“At the sink.”

“I waved at the window.”

“That’s all right,” she said. “It was open.”
